content.title: Joint project: reliable cross-script Serbian contract search

facts.text: The company estimates that roughly one in five searches was affected by cross-script misses in a January 2024 server-log sample. It attributes the problem to its PostgreSQL full-text index treating Cyrillic and Latin as different character sets.

sources.quote: We estimated this affects roughly one in five searches based on a sample we pulled from server logs in January 2024.
The root cause is that our full-text search index in PostgreSQL treats the two scripts as completely different character sets.

facts.text: The company's brief identifies mixed-script documents, dialect-dependent Latin-to-Cyrillic ambiguity and response-time sensitivity as concerns.

sources.quote: We want a solution that is robust enough to handle mixed-script documents, not just fully-Cyrillic or fully-Latin ones
there are edge cases where the same Latin sequence maps to different Cyrillic letters depending on dialect conventions.
does not slow down search response times noticeably.

facts.text: The company reports one backend engineer available for up to six weeks. Dragić's notes describe two active projects and capacity for one small industrial contract or consultancy.

sources.quote: We have one backend engineer who can work on this for up to six weeks.
Trenutno je angažovan na dva aktivna projekta, ali ima kapaciteta za jedan manji industrijski ugovor ili konsultantski angažman.

facts.text: Dragić states a preference for clearly defined, sufficiently large Serbian-language corpora and research-oriented collaboration rather than general software development.

sources.quote: Dragić preferira saradnju s kompanijama koje imaju jasno definisan i dovoljno veliki tekstualni korpus na srpskom jeziku
nije zainteresovan za opšte projekte razvoja softvera bez istraživačke komponente.

facts.text: The company's technology inventory lists PostgreSQL full-text search, Docker and Kubernetes in a Serbian private cloud, and a self-assessed ISO 27001-aligned internal security policy.

sources.quote: PostgreSQL with full-text search for document storage
Docker and Kubernetes on a private cloud hosted in Serbia

facts.text: Dragić's work evaluates phoneme-based canonicalization on court decisions. His separate latency study reports a tradeoff: transformer normalization improved retrieval quality but added 47 ms at the 99th percentile.

sources.quote: We evaluated the approach on a manually annotated gold standard of 4 200 query–document relevance pairs drawn from a legal corpus of 38 000 court decisions.
The transformer-based normalizer achieves MRR of 0.68 but adds 47 ms at the 99th percentile.

facts.text: Dragić lists openness to joint projects with companies managing large Serbian-language document collections.

sources.quote: joint projects with companies that manage large Serbian-language document collections

inferences: This suggests a focused joint project could resolve normalization placement rather than merely implement transliteration. Court-decision evidence does not validate contract retrieval, PostgreSQL compatibility or latency under this company's workload.

Canonicalization could conflate distinct legal terms; ambiguous digraphs, names and identifiers could remain failure sources. Neural fallback could add latency, while new terminology would likely require exception maintenance.

The proposal is conditional: joint-project openness is stated, but Dragić's start-date availability is unknown and his capacity is limited. The historical failure estimate may not describe current traffic or isolate script mismatch from parsing and morphology.
proposedActions: Propose a PostgreSQL sandbox experiment using company contracts and representative queries, with separate tuning and held-out evaluation samples whose independence is checked by grouping duplicate queries and related contracts. Compare unchanged search, index-only normalization, query-only normalization and both, holding parsing, morphology and ranking fixed. Propose Dragić designs canonicalization and exception tests; the company engineer integrates and replays representative load, with legal reviewers judging every evaluation query and candidate result. Include both cross-script directions, mixed-script documents, ambiguous mappings, names and identifiers. Select the best configuration on tuning data. Proposed go/no-go on held-out data: halve the zero-hit rate among queries with reviewer-confirmed existing relevant contracts, lose at most one percentage point in P@10, and add at most 5% to p95/p99 latency under matched load. Count each query execution once, without merging; use all confirmed-answerable executions as the failure-rate denominator. Require these criteria separately for mixed-script documents and cross-script directions. Unresolved cases count conservatively against acceptance; insufficient confidence or missing population data means no pass.

Propose week 1 for corpus sizing, access approval, current-failure reproduction and threshold negotiation; weeks 2–4 for the controlled comparison and tuning; weeks 5–6 for frozen evaluation and integration review. Agree sample sizes and confidence procedures before testing. Audit parsing failures separately, establish PostgreSQL tokenizer/index compatibility, and retain the placement comparison even if one configuration shows no benefit.

Keep experiments within approved private-cloud and security arrangements. Before proceeding, agree corpus sufficiency, reviewer capacity, tool licensing, budget, researcher hours, reindexing/storage limits and rollback. Measure actual integration effort and resource use; feasibility within the engineer's six-week allocation is an additional go/no-go gate. These are proposed procedures and targets, not agreed commitments.
questions: Can Dragić confirm availability, start date and time allocation for this small joint project within the company's six-week engineering window?
What corpus and query volumes, independent held-out mixed-script cases, legal reviewers and permitted contract/log access are available?
Which PostgreSQL configuration, production load and numerical interpretation of 'not noticeably slower' should govern acceptance?
Can both parties agree budget, responsibilities, security permissions, licensing, reindexing/storage limits and rollback before starting?

content.markdown:
# Joint project: reliable cross-script Serbian contract search

## Verified facts
- The company estimates that roughly one in five searches was affected by cross-script misses in a January 2024 server-log sample. It attributes the problem to its PostgreSQL full-text index treating Cyrillic and Latin as different character sets. [F1]
- The company's brief identifies mixed-script documents, dialect-dependent Latin-to-Cyrillic ambiguity and response-time sensitivity as concerns. [F2]
- The company reports one backend engineer available for up to six weeks. Dragić's notes describe two active projects and capacity for one small industrial contract or consultancy. [F3]
- Dragić states a preference for clearly defined, sufficiently large Serbian-language corpora and research-oriented collaboration rather than general software development. [F4]
- The company's technology inventory lists PostgreSQL full-text search, Docker and Kubernetes in a Serbian private cloud, and a self-assessed ISO 27001-aligned internal security policy. [F5]
- Dragić's work evaluates phoneme-based canonicalization on court decisions. His separate latency study reports a tradeoff: transformer normalization improved retrieval quality but added 47 ms at the 99th percentile. [F6]
- Dragić lists openness to joint projects with companies managing large Serbian-language document collections. [F7]

## Potential benefits
- For the company: The experiment could identify a practical normalization placement and quantify remaining missed matches, relevance losses and latency costs before deployment.
- For the researcher: Subject to agreement and permitted access, Dragić could test how canonicalization placement transfers from prior retrieval settings to mixed-script contracts in PostgreSQL, using company-specific relevance judgments and workload measurements.

## Our inference
- This suggests a focused joint project could resolve normalization placement rather than merely implement transliteration. Court-decision evidence does not validate contract retrieval, PostgreSQL compatibility or latency under this company's workload.
- Canonicalization could conflate distinct legal terms; ambiguous digraphs, names and identifiers could remain failure sources. Neural fallback could add latency, while new terminology would likely require exception maintenance.
- The proposal is conditional: joint-project openness is stated, but Dragić's start-date availability is unknown and his capacity is limited. The historical failure estimate may not describe current traffic or isolate script mismatch from parsing and morphology.

## Proposed next steps
- Propose a PostgreSQL sandbox experiment using company contracts and representative queries, with separate tuning and held-out evaluation samples whose independence is checked by grouping duplicate queries and related contracts. Compare unchanged search, index-only normalization, query-only normalization and both, holding parsing, morphology and ranking fixed. Propose Dragić designs canonicalization and exception tests; the company engineer integrates and replays representative load, with legal reviewers judging every evaluation query and candidate result. Include both cross-script directions, mixed-script documents, ambiguous mappings, names and identifiers. Select the best configuration on tuning data. Proposed go/no-go on held-out data: halve the zero-hit rate among queries with reviewer-confirmed existing relevant contracts, lose at most one percentage point in P@10, and add at most 5% to p95/p99 latency under matched load. Count each query execution once, without merging; use all confirmed-answerable executions as the failure-rate denominator. Require these criteria separately for mixed-script documents and cross-script directions. Unresolved cases count conservatively against acceptance; insufficient confidence or missing population data means no pass.
- Propose week 1 for corpus sizing, access approval, current-failure reproduction and threshold negotiation; weeks 2–4 for the controlled comparison and tuning; weeks 5–6 for frozen evaluation and integration review. Agree sample sizes and confidence procedures before testing. Audit parsing failures separately, establish PostgreSQL tokenizer/index compatibility, and retain the placement comparison even if one configuration shows no benefit.
- Keep experiments within approved private-cloud and security arrangements. Before proceeding, agree corpus sufficiency, reviewer capacity, tool licensing, budget, researcher hours, reindexing/storage limits and rollback. Measure actual integration effort and resource use; feasibility within the engineer's six-week allocation is an additional go/no-go gate. These are proposed procedures and targets, not agreed commitments.

## Open questions
- Can Dragić confirm availability, start date and time allocation for this small joint project within the company's six-week engineering window?
- What corpus and query volumes, independent held-out mixed-script cases, legal reviewers and permitted contract/log access are available?
- Which PostgreSQL configuration, production load and numerical interpretation of 'not noticeably slower' should govern acceptance?
- Can both parties agree budget, responsibilities, security permissions, licensing, reindexing/storage limits and rollback before starting?
